free_text: Measurement of the 9Be(p,n) thick target spectrum for
use in accelerator-based Boron Neutron Capture Therapy
Main Paper #1.
Additional Paper #2.
Additional Paper #3.
Additional Paper #4.
The T11 tandem Van de Graaff, and TOF
tunnel of the Ohio University Accelerator Laboratory.
Four to six lithium-loaded glass
scintillators. The lithium glass detectors contained
6.6% weight fraction of lithium, which was enriched
to 95% 6Li. The detectors were 1.27 cm thick and 12.7
cm in diameter. A detector array made up of seven
11.5-cm diameter x 5 cm thick NE213 scintillators.
The fission chamber used ultrapure methane as a
counting gas and was composed of four 235U foils:
The targets used were 2.5 cm square, and 0.25 and 0.5
mm thick, and 99.9% pure in their beryllium content.
These targets were thick enough to stop 4-MeV
protons. Neutrons produced at the target must pass
through a collimator with a 30-cm diameter in a
1.2-m-thick concrete wall before entering the flight
tunnel, which shields the flight path from neutrons
scattered near the source.
Standard TOF techniques were used in the
determination of neutron spectra. The axis of the
accelerator is perpendicular to the axis of the
flight tunnel, so the beam must be redirected by
using the beam swinger. The fixed detectors can be
set to record data for laboratory angles from -4 to
+160 deg simply by rotating the swinger. The target
chamber is mounted at the end of the beam swinger
gantry.
Statistical errors.
There is an additional 5% error in the
absolute normalization of the Al(d,n) spectra from
the uncertainty in the composition of the fission
foils used to determine the Al(d,n) spectrum at 7.44
MeV and 120 degrees.
